tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

content.content:
# Constitution

The rules the process itself is subject to. Specifications, designs, code and agents are
subordinate to this document; where anything below disagrees with it, this document wins.

Every article carries an enforcement level. **[CRITICAL]** blocks a merge, and an agent is to
stop and escalate rather than work around it. **[SHOULD]** is a strong default whose departure
needs a reason recorded in the change. **[MAY]** is guidance.

Changing an article requires an ADR in [`ADR/`](ADR/).

---

## Article I — The specification is the source of truth [CRITICAL]

Behaviour is described in `spec/` before it is built. Code contradicting `spec/` is either a
defect in the code or a change not applied to the specification. It is never an accepted
divergence, and "the code is the documentation" is not an answer this project accepts.

It is the specification, not the code, that the next person reads at three in the morning. The
code says what happens; only the specification says what was *meant* to happen — and that is the
only thing that lets anybody tell a feature from a bug.

## Article II — Requirements are testable sentences with identifiers [CRITICAL]

A requirement uses the EARS keywords — `WHEN`, `WHILE`, `IF … THEN`, `WHERE` — together with
`MUST` or `SHALL`. Never *should*, *may*, *could*, *probably* or *etc.* A requirement that
cannot be failed cannot be satisfied.

Every requirement carries a unique identifier scoped by its change (`CR-2608-a7f3/R-3`) and
every one has acceptance criteria written as Given/When/Then. A criterion no observer could
check is not a criterion.

## Article III — Every requirement is proved by a test [CRITICAL]

No requirement travels without at least one test that refers to it by identifier. The reference
is mechanical — a `req` marker, a Gherkin tag or the identifier in a test's name — and the
`specs` gate checks both directions: a requirement nothing refers to fails, and a reference to a
requirement that does not exist also fails. The second half matters more than the first, because
a typo is what every traceability scheme actually dies of.

Where a requirement genuinely cannot be tested automatically, it says so about itself in its own
text (`**Verified-by:** manual — <reason>`). The exception is then counted and printed, and that
is the difference between a gap considered and a gap passed over.

## Article IV — The specification changes on the same branch as the code [CRITICAL]

A change of behaviour and the specification edit that describes it land in one pull request.
Never in the next one. The next one guarantees a window in which the trunk describes code that
no longer exists, and it rests on a step nobody is blocked by.

Every edit under `spec/` is declared in that change's `delta.md` as `ADDED` / `MODIFIED` /
`REMOVED` together with a `**Why:**`. The declared set and the actual diff must be *equal* — an
edit absent from the delta fails, and a delta entry with no edit also fails.

## Article V — Non-goals are written down [SHOULD]

Every change says what it deliberately does **not** do. Silent scope is what makes a reviewer
and an author finish agreeing about two different things, and what turns a "missing" feature
into an argument six months later rather than a decision anybody remembers.

## Article VI — A rule the database does not hold is not a rule [CRITICAL]

A constraint the application relies on and the storage layer does not enforce is a constraint
that falls over under concurrency. Business uniqueness is a unique index rather than a
convention: a rule checked by read-before-write passes every sequential test and lets two
concurrent requests through. The same principle governs every boundary: the contract is the
authority and the code is validated against it, not the other way round.

## Article VII — Ambiguity is a question, never an improvisation [CRITICAL]

Where a requirement, a field, a label or a rule is unclear, the process stops and asks a human.
It does not pick the more likely reading and does not rationalise the choice in an artefact
where the next reader will take it for a decision.

The question is closed — two to four options, the recommendation first, each with its
consequence in one sentence — with free text always available. A free-text answer is
interpreted, announced and recorded; it never produces the same question a second time.

## Article VIII — A divergence is a measurement and it edits the specification [CRITICAL]

Independent artefacts are produced in parallel from one specification, and a disagreement
between them is not an accident to patch. It is a measurement of where the specification was
ambiguous.

Every settled disagreement is followed by an edit to the *earliest* document which, had it been
clearer, would have prevented it. Fixing only the artefact at the end of the chain leaves the
ambiguity in place, and the next change walks into it again.

A ruling may be taken automatically **only** when it follows from a document higher in the
hierarchy, and the record must name that document and section:

```
constitution.md  >  invariants.md  ~  contracts/invariants/  >  design/**  >  a change's requirements  >  a change's design
```

`invariants.md` and `contracts/invariants/` stand on the **same rung**, because after the move
they are two halves of one document: the first holds the deliberate non-goals and the rule about
the rules themselves, the second the data invariants. The order between them is arbitrary and
stays that way until the first case in which a non-goal and a data invariant contradict each
other; then a human decides, not this arrow.

Everything else is a product decision and belongs to a human.

## Article IX — The why is recorded where it cannot be edited out [CRITICAL]

A decision is an ADR when it rejects a named alternative **and** is cross-cutting — reversing it
touches more than one module, layer or suite — **and** is expensive to reverse: undoing it needs
a data migration, a rewritten contract or a change in CI, not an edit to one file. An ADR is
dated, numbered, never rewritten, and superseded only by a later ADR. Normative documents state
the rule in the present tense and link to it.

A decision that only rejects an alternative is also recorded and has its address: a fact always
true of the data goes to `contracts/invariants/`, a deliberate non-goal to `spec/invariants.md`,
a placement or naming rule to `spec/design/conventions.md`, the choice of a suite or a fixture
to `spec/design/testing.md`, a column or a constraint to `spec/design/data-model.md`, a contract
field or a refusal code to `spec/design/api.md`. All five are normative, so the rule binds
exactly as hard as it would in `ADR/` — it merely stops costing a row in an index everybody has
to read before writing the next decision. The threshold and the table of homes:
[`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § When a decision is an ADR.

Beside ADRs, **intent** is recorded in the code itself: a non-obvious rule carries the reason it
exists, and where there was an incident — that incident. This project already writes that way —
[`scripts/check.sh`](../scripts/check.sh) names the failure behind every gate it runs — and it is
the main defence against somebody "simplifying" a rule whose cost is invisible from a diff.

Module docstrings cite the specification: `spec/design/data-model.md`, `BR-02`, `P-01`,
`CR-2608-a7f3/R-3`. Keep that density.

## Article X — Between two steps the application works [CRITICAL]

After every stage the full gate runs and must be green. A stage never ends red.

The only exception is a failure the process created deliberately: a test written before its
implementation. Such a failure is declared *before* the run that shows it, must be proved to
have actually occurred, and expires. A declaration made after seeing the failure, or a declared
failure the runner does not even collect, fails the gate — otherwise deleting a failing test
reads exactly like fixing it.

## Article XI — Personal data does not leave the machine that needs it [CRITICAL]

This template holds no personal data today — a guestbook entry is a signature somebody gave
themselves. A product built from it will hold some, and an assertion message can quote every
value a test saw. That is the reason [`pyproject.toml`](../pyproject.toml) sets
`junit_logging = "no"` and the reason no committed artefact — a state file, a report, a change
record — carries the text of a test failure. Identities and counts, never contents.

One exception, and it is named rather than implied: `spec/changes/*/sessions/**` holds raw Claude
Code transcripts, deliberately unsanitised, so that the process can be studied from what actually
happened. The archive counts the shapes of personal data it carries and refuses to hide that
count; the price is that nothing may be pasted into an SDD session that is not to live in that
history forever. The exception extends to that path and to nothing else.

Authentication, personal data and every regulated surface require a human decision. An agent
escalates; it never merges such a change on its own.

## Article XII — The project's scripts are the interface [CRITICAL]

Every task is a script. Run the script, never a command from inside it: each checks its own
prerequisites, and those checks exist because their absence produced failures that took a day to
find. `scripts/check.sh` is the definition of "will CI pass" — a gate added to CI belongs there
too, and a fitness function proves the two lists are equal rather than believing they are.

There are two interfaces, and which directory a script sits in says which one it is.

[`scripts/`](../scripts/) is the **human's** interface to the application — running, testing,
linting, migrating. Run by a person or by CI. Every task exists there as **one** `.sh` script
over the shared `_lib.sh`; task scripts written in Python are libraries that the `.sh` calls,
not a second entry point to the same task.

The scripts are POSIX and that is a decision rather than neglect
([`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § Scripts). Windows is supported through WSL
or Git Bash and through nothing else; a named absence of support is more honest than a second
copy of every script that diverges in the week nobody is looking at it.

[the engine](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/skills/_shared/sdd/) is the **agent's** interface to
the change *process*. Called by the skills that name it, from the repository root, one
implementation per platform. It ships with those skills — in the plugin, not in this
repository — so that a skill and the script it calls change together, and `skill_lint.py`
breaks the build when they do not. The process's own
commands under [the process's own `bin/`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/bin/) are the bridge — its CI runs a shell script, and
the shell script runs Python. `scripts/` is the application's interface and never calls the
process; what the process may call in `scripts/` is the script contract
([`script-contract.md`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/docs/script-contract.md)).

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-09, `cr: historical` — the process became independent of the
application it works on: a template ships `scripts/` and a stack profile, the process ships
the process's own commands and reads the profile; two trees, two CIs, one contract between them): a script
in `scripts/` as the bridge from the application's CI into the process. It made the application
depend on the process, in the one direction the split forbids, and it put a gate the process
owns into a list the template's CI keeps.

Neither directory is a place to opt out of anything. Both are covered by `ruff` and
`mypy --strict`; choosing a folder has never been a way to lower the standard here.

## Article XIII — Allowed and forbidden [CRITICAL]

**Allowed.** Python ≥ 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.0 with Alembic, Pydantic 2, PostgreSQL 16 and
only it ([`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md) § One engine), `uv` in the range
`>=0.12,<0.13`; TypeScript 5.9, React 19, Vite, TanStack Query, react-hook-form with zod,
Tailwind 4 over CSS design tokens; pytest, pytest-bdd, vitest, testcontainers; Playwright
(Chromium alone) only in `e2e/ui/` — [`design/testing.md`](design/testing.md) § The UI smoke in
a browser.

**Forbidden.** Business logic in routers. `fastapi` or `starlette` imported from `services/`,
`models/` or `schemas/`. `create_all()`. A raw hex colour or a magic pixel size in a component.
A file named `utils.py`, `helpers.py`, `common.py`, `format.ts` or `utils.ts`. Star imports,
with one mechanical exception documented in
[`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md). Unpinned tool versions in a gate. Logging
secrets, tokens or personal data.

## Where the process's own files are named

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-09, `cr: historical` — the change process left this repository
for the plugin `forge@scalo`. Article XII still holds word for word: a tool the stack
profile refuses is not run by hand, and the process's own commands are the bridge from the
process into Python. What changed is only where those commands come from — they arrive on
PATH with the plugin instead of sitting in a directory of this repository's — so the article's links now name
the repository that ships them. No article was reworded; `spec/ADR/` stays empty until the
first change goes through `/forge:sdd`, and framework changes are made on the trunk and carry no
`delta.md`): rewording Article XII to describe a plugin. The article is about not assembling
commands by hand, which is true of every layout, and an article edited to track a directory
would need editing again at the next move.
-----
# When the process is the thing that is broken

*A shared contract. The worker contract quotes it as rule 15, and the injected session context
as iron rule 12, instead of describing it in words of their own.*

---

## The principle

> **Working around the process is a finding ABOUT the process. Where the fault cannot be fixed
> from the tree you are standing in, the finding is a ticket — filed at the moment you have the
> evidence, not at the end of the session that had it.**

The process already knows how to be wrong loudly: a gate goes red, a hook refuses, a skill
returns `FAILED`. What it did not know how to be is wrong *quietly* — a rule bent rather than
broken, a step improvised because none was written, a script run once to get past something.
Every one of those passes every gate, and every one of them is the process telling you
something it has no other way to say.

Which repository can fix it is not a judgement: `sdd-ownership` answers it. Whose fault it is
*is* a judgement, and § 8 of the intake form is where you argue it.

## The signals

### Measured — the session audit already counts these

`session_audit.py` names them from a transcript, hours later. Meeting one *while you are
working* is the same finding, earlier and with the evidence still in hand.

| What it counts | What it means |
|---|---|
| `improvisation -- code written in the command rather than in a file` | a `python3 -c`, a `node -e`, a heredoc fed to an interpreter: code with no file, no test and no second reader |
| `improvisation -- a script written on the fly instead of a verb` | you wrote a `.py` or `.sh` to get past something, and the process has a verb for it or ought to |
| `improvisation -- a program in argv` | a chain of commands long enough to be a program somebody will have to read once and never again |
| `art. XII --` | a tool the stack profile refuses, run directly rather than through the script that wraps it |

And the four hatches, which are **counted rather than forbidden**. Each is a legitimate move
that somebody signed for. A hatch used once is a decision; a hatch used as a road is the
finding, and the second time is when to say so.

| What it counts | The move |
|---|---|
| `escape hatch -- a stage closed on a red gate` | `--accept-red` |
| `escape hatch -- lowering the path below the arithmetic` | `--allow-lower` |
| `escape hatch -- preempting the change slot` | `--force-parallel-hotfix` |
| `escape hatch -- the question queue was skipped` | `ask --now` |

### Judged — no pattern catches these, and they are the ones that cost most

- **You improvised a step.** The stage said what to produce and no skill said how, so you
  decided. That decision was not reviewed by anybody and is now in the artefact.
- **You rationalised a rule into not applying here.** `verification.md` already names the
  shape: *"I will use different words and the rule will not apply."* If the argument for
  skipping something took more than one sentence, that is the signal.
- **You repaired the process to get the task done.** You edited a skill, a gate, a profile or
  a script because it was in your way. Whether or not the edit was right, the task was the
  reason — and a repair whose reason was impatience is a repair nobody reviewed.
- **An instruction named something that is not there.** A skill told you to read a file, run a
  command or cite a document that does not exist on this stack. An instruction that cannot be
  carried out is not a thing to route around; inventing the missing input is how fabricated
  data gets into an artefact.
- **The same failure twice.** The orchestrator already calls this out — *"the same failure
  twice is not an iteration"* — and the second time is the finding, not the third.

## Which document wins

Two live documents used to give opposite orders and nothing ranked them. **This one wins, and
the worker contract with it.** A project's own `CLAUDE.md` — a template's, or an instance's —
describes its tree; it does not get to say who in this process may post outward, because the
half that may is a property of the process and not of the stack. Where a `CLAUDE.md` says *file
it immediately*, it is describing **the orchestrator's half**, which is true, and it is not
addressing a dispatched worker, which cannot.

And the label is **never** a thing a document writes down. `sdd-ownership` computes it from
GitHub's own record of the lineage — `from-template` from a template, `from-instance` from an
instance — so a `--label` written into an instruction is a value that was right once. Fourteen
issues in this register carry `from-template` and were raised from an instance repository; that
is what a typed label looks like a year later, and it is why no verb below takes one.

## What you do

Three steps, in this order. They cost one command and one paragraph.

1. **Bank it, then file it — and do not stop to ask.** Banking is first because it cannot fail:

   ```bash
   sdd-engine change_state add-fault --cr <CR> --signal '<what it did, and what it cost>' \
     --owner engine
   ```

   `--owner` is the judgement and it takes one of three words: `engine`, `template`, or `here`
   for a fault this level owns and repairs rather than files.
   It writes the fault into the change record with the destination and its label **computed**,
   allocates it a `PROC-n`, and refuses nothing for want of a network. A second report of the
   same fault inside one change is the same row with `seen` counted up, not a second ticket.
   Then `fault-report` fills the form and runs one `gh issue create` against the address that
   was computed, and:

   ```bash
   sdd-engine change_state resolve-fault --cr <CR> --id PROC-n --filed <url>
   ```

   Do not search for a duplicate first — a duplicate costs a close and a link, a report lost
   with the session that found it costs the evidence. This is the intake rule that already
   governs a template filing upward, and it governs this for the same reason.

# Constitution

The rules the process itself is subject to. Specifications, designs, code and agents are
subordinate to this document; where anything below disagrees with it, this document wins.

Every article carries an enforcement level. **[CRITICAL]** blocks a merge, and an agent is to
stop and escalate rather than work around it. **[SHOULD]** is a strong default whose departure
needs a reason recorded in the change. **[MAY]** is guidance.

Changing an article requires an ADR in [`ADR/`](ADR/).

---

## Article I — The specification is the source of truth [CRITICAL]

Behaviour is described in `spec/` before it is built. Code contradicting `spec/` is either a
defect in the code or a change not applied to the specification. It is never an accepted
divergence, and "the code is the documentation" is not an answer this project accepts.

It is the specification, not the code, that the next person reads at three in the morning. The
code says what happens; only the specification says what was *meant* to happen — and that is the
only thing that lets anybody tell a feature from a bug.

## Article II — Requirements are testable sentences with identifiers [CRITICAL]

A requirement uses the EARS keywords — `WHEN`, `WHILE`, `IF … THEN`, `WHERE` — together with
`MUST` or `SHALL`. Never *should*, *may*, *could*, *probably* or *etc.* A requirement that
cannot be failed cannot be satisfied.

Every requirement carries a unique identifier scoped by its change (`CR-2608-a7f3/R-3`) and
every one has acceptance criteria written as Given/When/Then. A criterion no observer could
check is not a criterion.

## Article III — Every requirement is proved by a test [CRITICAL]

No requirement travels without at least one test that refers to it by identifier. The reference
is mechanical — a `req` marker, a Gherkin tag or the identifier in a test's name — and the
`specs` gate checks both directions: a requirement nothing refers to fails, and a reference to a
requirement that does not exist also fails. The second half matters more than the first, because
a typo is what every traceability scheme actually dies of.

Where a requirement genuinely cannot be tested automatically, it says so about itself in its own
text (`**Verified-by:** manual — <reason>`). The exception is then counted and printed, and that
is the difference between a gap considered and a gap passed over.

## Article IV — The specification changes on the same branch as the code [CRITICAL]

A change of behaviour and the specification edit that describes it land in one pull request.
Never in the next one. The next one guarantees a window in which the trunk describes code that
no longer exists, and it rests on a step nobody is blocked by.

Every edit under `spec/` is declared in that change's `delta.md` as `ADDED` / `MODIFIED` /
`REMOVED` together with a `**Why:**`. The declared set and the actual diff must be *equal* — an
edit absent from the delta fails, and a delta entry with no edit also fails.

## Article V — Non-goals are written down [SHOULD]

Every change says what it deliberately does **not** do. Silent scope is what makes a reviewer
and an author finish agreeing about two different things, and what turns a "missing" feature
into an argument six months later rather than a decision anybody remembers.

## Article VI — A rule the database does not hold is not a rule [CRITICAL]

A constraint the application relies on and the storage layer does not enforce is a constraint
that falls over under concurrency. Business uniqueness is a unique index rather than a
convention: a rule checked by read-before-write passes every sequential test and lets two
concurrent requests through. The same principle governs every boundary: the contract is the
authority and the code is validated against it, not the other way round.

## Article VII — Ambiguity is a question, never an improvisation [CRITICAL]

Where a requirement, a field, a label or a rule is unclear, the process stops and asks a human.
It does not pick the more likely reading and does not rationalise the choice in an artefact
where the next reader will take it for a decision.

The question is closed — two to four options, the recommendation first, each with its
consequence in one sentence — with free text always available. A free-text answer is
interpreted, announced and recorded; it never produces the same question a second time.

## Article VIII — A divergence is a measurement and it edits the specification [CRITICAL]

Independent artefacts are produced in parallel from one specification, and a disagreement
between them is not an accident to patch. It is a measurement of where the specification was
ambiguous.

Every settled disagreement is followed by an edit to the *earliest* document which, had it been
clearer, would have prevented it. Fixing only the artefact at the end of the chain leaves the
ambiguity in place, and the next change walks into it again.

A ruling may be taken automatically **only** when it follows from a document higher in the
hierarchy, and the record must name that document and section:

```
constitution.md  >  invariants.md  ~  contracts/invariants/  >  design/**  >  a change's requirements  >  a change's design
```

`invariants.md` and `contracts/invariants/` stand on the **same rung**, because after the move
they are two halves of one document: the first holds the deliberate non-goals and the rule about
the rules themselves, the second the data invariants. The order between them is arbitrary and
stays that way until the first case in which a non-goal and a data invariant contradict each
other; then a human decides, not this arrow.

Everything else is a product decision and belongs to a human.

## Article IX — The why is recorded where it cannot be edited out [CRITICAL]

A decision is an ADR when it rejects a named alternative **and** is cross-cutting — reversing it
touches more than one module, layer or suite — **and** is expensive to reverse: undoing it needs
a data migration, a rewritten contract or a change in CI, not an edit to one file. An ADR is
dated, numbered, never rewritten, and superseded only by a later ADR. Normative documents state
the rule in the present tense and link to it.

A decision that only rejects an alternative is also recorded and has its address: a fact always
true of the data goes to `contracts/invariants/`, a deliberate non-goal to `spec/invariants.md`,
a placement or naming rule to `spec/design/conventions.md`, the choice of a suite or a fixture
to `spec/design/testing.md`, a column or a constraint to `spec/design/data-model.md`, a contract
field or a refusal code to `spec/design/api.md`. All five are normative, so the rule binds
exactly as hard as it would in `ADR/` — it merely stops costing a row in an index everybody has
to read before writing the next decision. The threshold and the table of homes:
[`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § When a decision is an ADR.

Beside ADRs, **intent** is recorded in the code itself: a non-obvious rule carries the reason it
exists, and where there was an incident — that incident. This project already writes that way —
[`scripts/check.sh`](../scripts/check.sh) names the failure behind every gate it runs — and it is
the main defence against somebody "simplifying" a rule whose cost is invisible from a diff.

Module docstrings cite the specification: `spec/design/data-model.md`, `BR-02`, `P-01`,
`CR-2608-a7f3/R-3`. Keep that density.

## Article X — Between two steps the application works [CRITICAL]

After every stage the full gate runs and must be green. A stage never ends red.

The only exception is a failure the process created deliberately: a test written before its
implementation. Such a failure is declared *before* the run that shows it, must be proved to
have actually occurred, and expires. A declaration made after seeing the failure, or a declared
failure the runner does not even collect, fails the gate — otherwise deleting a failing test
reads exactly like fixing it.

## Article XI — Personal data does not leave the machine that needs it [CRITICAL]

This template holds no personal data today — a guestbook entry is a signature somebody gave
themselves. A product built from it will hold some, and an assertion message can quote every
value a test saw. That is the reason [`pyproject.toml`](../pyproject.toml) sets
`junit_logging = "no"` and the reason no committed artefact — a state file, a report, a change
record — carries the text of a test failure. Identities and counts, never contents.

One exception, and it is named rather than implied: `spec/changes/*/sessions/**` holds raw Claude
Code transcripts, deliberately unsanitised, so that the process can be studied from what actually
happened. The archive counts the shapes of personal data it carries and refuses to hide that
count; the price is that nothing may be pasted into an SDD session that is not to live in that
history forever. The exception extends to that path and to nothing else.

Authentication, personal data and every regulated surface require a human decision. An agent
escalates; it never merges such a change on its own.

## Article XII — The project's scripts are the interface [CRITICAL]

Every task is a script. Run the script, never a command from inside it: each checks its own
prerequisites, and those checks exist because their absence produced failures that took a day to
find. `scripts/check.sh` is the definition of "will CI pass" — a gate added to CI belongs there
too, and a fitness function proves the two lists are equal rather than believing they are.

There are two interfaces, and which directory a script sits in says which one it is.

[`scripts/`](../scripts/) is the **human's** interface to the application — running, testing,
linting, migrating. Run by a person or by CI. Every task exists there as **one** `.sh` script
over the shared `_lib.sh`; task scripts written in Python are libraries that the `.sh` calls,
not a second entry point to the same task.

The scripts are POSIX and that is a decision rather than neglect
([`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § Scripts). Windows is supported through WSL
or Git Bash and through nothing else; a named absence of support is more honest than a second
copy of every script that diverges in the week nobody is looking at it.

[the engine](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/skills/_shared/sdd/) is the **agent's** interface to
the change *process*. Called by the skills that name it, from the repository root, one
implementation per platform. It ships with those skills — in the plugin, not in this
repository — so that a skill and the script it calls change together, and `skill_lint.py`
breaks the build when they do not. The process's own
commands under [the process's own `bin/`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/bin/) are the bridge — its CI runs a shell script, and
the shell script runs Python. `scripts/` is the application's interface and never calls the
process; what the process may call in `scripts/` is the script contract
([`script-contract.md`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/docs/script-contract.md)).

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-09, `cr: historical` — the process became independent of the
application it works on: a template ships `scripts/` and a stack profile, the process ships
the process's own commands and reads the profile; two trees, two CIs, one contract between them): a script
in `scripts/` as the bridge from the application's CI into the process. It made the application
depend on the process, in the one direction the split forbids, and it put a gate the process
owns into a list the template's CI keeps.

Neither directory is a place to opt out of anything. Both are covered by `ruff` and
`mypy --strict`; choosing a folder has never been a way to lower the standard here.

## Article XIII — Allowed and forbidden [CRITICAL]

**Allowed.** Python ≥ 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2.0 with Alembic, Pydantic 2, PostgreSQL 16 and
only it ([`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md) § One engine), `uv` in the range
`>=0.12,<0.13`; TypeScript 5.9, React 19, Vite, TanStack Query, react-hook-form with zod,
Tailwind 4 over CSS design tokens; pytest, pytest-bdd, vitest, testcontainers; Playwright
(Chromium alone) only in `e2e/ui/` — [`design/testing.md`](design/testing.md) § The UI smoke in
a browser.

**Forbidden.** Business logic in routers. `fastapi` or `starlette` imported from `services/`,
`models/` or `schemas/`. `create_all()`. A raw hex colour or a magic pixel size in a component.
A file named `utils.py`, `helpers.py`, `common.py`, `format.ts` or `utils.ts`. Star imports,
with one mechanical exception documented in
[`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md). Unpinned tool versions in a gate. Logging
secrets, tokens or personal data.

## Where the process's own files are named

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-09, `cr: historical` — the change process left this repository
for the plugin `forge@scalo`. Article XII still holds word for word: a tool the stack
profile refuses is not run by hand, and the process's own commands are the bridge from the
process into Python. What changed is only where those commands come from — they arrive on
PATH with the plugin instead of sitting in a directory of this repository's — so the article's links now name
the repository that ships them. No article was reworded; `spec/ADR/` stays empty until the
first change goes through `/forge:sdd`, and framework changes are made on the trunk and carry no
`delta.md`): rewording Article XII to describe a plugin. The article is about not assembling
commands by hand, which is true of every layout, and an article edited to track a directory
would need editing again at the next move.
-----
# When the process is the thing that is broken

*A shared contract. The worker contract quotes it as rule 15, and the injected session context
as iron rule 12, instead of describing it in words of their own.*

---

## The principle

> **Working around the process is a finding ABOUT the process. Where the fault cannot be fixed
> from the tree you are standing in, the finding is a ticket — filed at the moment you have the
> evidence, not at the end of the session that had it.**

The process already knows how to be wrong loudly: a gate goes red, a hook refuses, a skill
returns `FAILED`. What it did not know how to be is wrong *quietly* — a rule bent rather than
broken, a step improvised because none was written, a script run once to get past something.
Every one of those passes every gate, and every one of them is the process telling you
something it has no other way to say.

Which repository can fix it is not a judgement: `sdd-ownership` answers it. Whose fault it is
*is* a judgement, and § 8 of the intake form is where you argue it.

## The signals

### Measured — the session audit already counts these

`session_audit.py` names them from a transcript, hours later. Meeting one *while you are
working* is the same finding, earlier and with the evidence still in hand.

| What it counts | What it means |
|---|---|
| `improvisation -- code written in the command rather than in a file` | a `python3 -c`, a `node -e`, a heredoc fed to an interpreter: code with no file, no test and no second reader |
| `improvisation -- a script written on the fly instead of a verb` | you wrote a `.py` or `.sh` to get past something, and the process has a verb for it or ought to |
| `improvisation -- a program in argv` | a chain of commands long enough to be a program somebody will have to read once and never again |
| `art. XII --` | a tool the stack profile refuses, run directly rather than through the script that wraps it |

And the four hatches, which are **counted rather than forbidden**. Each is a legitimate move
that somebody signed for. A hatch used once is a decision; a hatch used as a road is the
finding, and the second time is when to say so.

| What it counts | The move |
|---|---|
| `escape hatch -- a stage closed on a red gate` | `--accept-red` |
| `escape hatch -- lowering the path below the arithmetic` | `--allow-lower` |
| `escape hatch -- preempting the change slot` | `--force-parallel-hotfix` |
| `escape hatch -- the question queue was skipped` | `ask --now` |

### Judged — no pattern catches these, and they are the ones that cost most

- **You improvised a step.** The stage said what to produce and no skill said how, so you
  decided. That decision was not reviewed by anybody and is now in the artefact.
- **You rationalised a rule into not applying here.** `verification.md` already names the
  shape: *"I will use different words and the rule will not apply."* If the argument for
  skipping something took more than one sentence, that is the signal.
- **You repaired the process to get the task done.** You edited a skill, a gate, a profile or
  a script because it was in your way. Whether or not the edit was right, the task was the
  reason — and a repair whose reason was impatience is a repair nobody reviewed.
- **An instruction named something that is not there.** A skill told you to read a file, run a
  command or cite a document that does not exist on this stack. An instruction that cannot be
  carried out is not a thing to route around; inventing the missing input is how fabricated
  data gets into an artefact.
- **The same failure twice.** The orchestrator already calls this out — *"the same failure
  twice is not an iteration"* — and the second time is the finding, not the third.

Two live documents used to give opposite orders and nothing ranked them. **This one wins, and
the worker contract with it.** A project's own `CLAUDE.md` — a template's, or an instance's —
describes its tree; it does not get to say who in this process may post outward, because the
half that may is a property of the process and not of the stack. Where a `CLAUDE.md` says *file
it immediately*, it is describing **the orchestrator's half**, which is true, and it is not
addressing a dispatched worker, which cannot.

And the label is **never** a thing a document writes down. `sdd-ownership` computes it from
GitHub's own record of the lineage — `from-template` from a template, `from-instance` from an
instance — so a `--label` written into an instruction is a value that was right once. Fourteen

# SDD Intake

<prerequisites>
## PREREQUISITES

### Stage 1 — Automated checks

    sdd-skill cr-request preflight

**Read what it prints; do not parse it, do not pipe it, do not truncate it.** It gives the
branch, the change this branch carries, the work slot, and the exact next call for this
skill. Session `ae3bb199` ran the raw envelope through `head -60` instead — which cuts a
JSON document into something no parser accepts — because the document here told it to parse
JSON.

### Stage 2 — Preparation

**In ONE message, issue ALL these Read calls in parallel:**

- `spec/contexts/` — what the product does, so the request can be placed
- the `§ Deliberate non-goals` sections under `spec/contexts/` and `spec/changes/INDEX.md` — what is built,
  specified, or deliberately absent
- `spec/glossary.md` — so the change is named in the words the team already uses

Do **not** read the code here. Understanding how it works today is the next skill's job,
and doing it now produces a scope guess before anyone has looked.
</prerequisites>

<iron_rules>
## IRON RULES

0. **Read `spec/invariants.md` § Deliberate non-goals in full before Phase 2.**
   A request that is already a recorded non-goal is the single most valuable thing to catch
   here, and the answer is a conversation rather than a change.
1. **Capture the request verbatim, in the user's own words, before anything else.** Not summarised, not
   translated, not tidied. `request.md` is the input the whole process interprets, and an
   interpretation written into it is an interpretation nobody can go back and check.
2. **Do not scope.** You are not deciding what the change includes. You are recording what
   was asked and creating somewhere to put the answer.
3. **Ask only what you cannot proceed without.** Two things decide what happens next — is
   this one change or several, and does it touch a screen — plus the parent, when the change
   corrects a merged CR and `INDEX.md` leaves it ambiguous. Everything else is the
   requirements stage's job, with the code in front of it. The count is the engine's, not
   this document's:
   [`/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/question-policy.md`](../_shared/question-policy.md).
4. **The baseline is taken before the first edit.** It is the definition of "already
   broken", and taken later it silently absolves this change of what it breaks.
5. **Never start a change on the trunk.** `cr.py` cuts the branch; work on the trunk is
   work with nowhere to undo it.

The first ninety seconds of a change decide whether the rest of it is about the user's
problem or about a guess somebody made early.
</iron_rules>

<role>
## ROLE

You are the person who **takes the request** — a colleague at the next desk, not a form.

**Expertise:**
- Getting a request written down in the asker's own words
- Recognising when one sentence is really three changes
- Placing a request against what the product already does

**Mindset:**
- **Their words are the specification's raw material.** Every rewrite loses something, and
  the thing lost is usually the reason they asked.
- **You are not solving it.** The temptation to say "ah, you want X" is exactly the
  improvisation this framework exists to prevent — and X arrives with a scope nobody chose.
- **A request that is already a non-goal deserves a conversation, not a branch.** Saying
  "this was deliberately left out, here is why" is a better outcome than a change.
</role>

<mandatory_todowrite>
## MANDATORY TODOWRITE

<context>
## PURPOSE & CONTEXT

**Context.** Someone in the back office has hit something: a column they cannot see, a file
the system refuses, a number that looks wrong. They describe it in their own words, in the middle of
their day, in whatever words come out.

**Goal.** Turn that into a change that exists — a directory, a branch, a record and a
baseline — without deciding anything about what it will contain.

**What this skill catches:**
- A request that is already a recorded non-goal, with a reason
- One sentence that is really three changes, before three become one tangle
- A defect in something delivered but not yet merged, which is a review fix rather than a
  new change
- A defect in a **merged** change that is not urgent, which is a `fix` with `--parent` —
  the full pipeline, correcting the parent's specification first
- A production problem that cannot wait, which is a hotfix against a merged change
</context>

<input_parsing>
## INPUT PARSING

Three doors, and which one opens depends on where the user stands and what they hold:

| What the user says | Kind |
|---|---|
| "I want it to be possible to…", "there is no…", "let us add…" | `feature` |
| "it computes wrongly", "it does not save", "it throws an error" — in something never delivered | `fix` |
| "there is a bug in CR-X", "what went in with change X works badly" **and HEAD is the trunk, not urgent** | `fix` with `--parent CR-X` — the pipeline runs in full, correcting the parent's spec first, then its design, then the code |
| "let us rename the column", "let us tidy up…" | `chore` |
| "X is broken in production, FIX IT NOW" **and HEAD is the trunk** | `hotfix` — hand to `sdd-hotfix-scope` |
| "what I tested yesterday does not work" **and a change is open on this branch** | not a new change — `review_fix`, the `sdd` orchestrator routes it |

For the `--parent` door: find the parent in `spec/changes/INDEX.md` by what the user calls
it. When two entries could match, that is the one extra closed question this skill may ask.
The difference between the last two rows is urgency, and it is the user's to declare: a
hotfix ships the smallest safe repair; a `fix` with a parent re-runs the whole pipeline
against the parent's specification.

**Does it touch a screen?** If the answer is yes, `--touches-ui`, and the design stage will
expect a Claude Design mock-up at `design/ui/index.html`. Ask if it is not obvious;
guessing wrong costs a whole design fan-out.
</input_parsing>

<quick_reference>
## QUICK REFERENCE

| Resource | Location |
|---|---|
| Create the change | `sdd-engine cr new "<title>" --request "<verbatim>" --tier {p0\|p1\|p2\|p3}` |
| Fix to a merged change | `… --kind fix --parent CR-YYMM-xxxx` |
| Take the baseline | `sdd-engine gate run --profile boundary --json --out .sdd/reports/baseline.json` |
| Record it | `sdd-engine change_state set-baseline --cr {cr} --from-file .sdd/reports/baseline.json` |
| The drop-folder checklist | `spec/changes/<CR>/input/README.md` (written by the scaffold) |
| Question payload safety | `sdd-engine hitl_text --text "<raw>"` |
| Non-goals | `spec/invariants.md` |
| What is already specified | `spec/contexts/`, `spec/changes/INDEX.md` |
| The merged changes, by title | `spec/changes/INDEX.md` |
</quick_reference>

<common_rationalizations>
## COMMON RATIONALIZATIONS

| Excuse | Reality |
|---|---|
| "I'll write a cleaner version of what they said" | Then the process interprets your sentence, not theirs, and nobody can tell the difference later. Quote them. |
| "I can see what they actually need" | Maybe. Write down what they said, and let the requirements stage — which will have read the code — find out. |
| "This is obviously two changes, I'll split it" | Ask. Splitting is a decision about how they will test and release it, and that is theirs. |
| "The baseline can wait until after the first commit" | Then everything already broken becomes this change's fault, and the person who opened it spends a day on somebody else's defect. |
| "It probably touches the UI, I'll set the flag to be safe" | That commits the design stage to expecting a mock-up nobody made. Ask. |
| "They're in a hurry, I'll skip straight to requirements" | Requirements without a branch has nowhere to put anything, and without a baseline no way to tell what it broke. |
</common_rationalizations>

<integration>
## INTEGRATION

### Tools used
- `Read` — the three product documents
- `AskUserQuestion` — closed questions, within the stage's budget
- `Bash` — `cr.py`, `gate.py`, `change_state.py`
- `Write` — nothing directly; `cr.py` writes `request.md`

### Files written
- `spec/changes/CR-YYMM-xxxx-<slug>/` — the whole directory, by `cr.py`
- `request.md` — the verbatim request
- `input/README.md` + the artifact templates — by the scaffold, each opening with the
  `TEMPLATE` marker that keeps a copied form from counting as a produced document
- `change.json` — the record, with the baseline

### Dependencies
A clean working tree. The container daemon the stack profile names
(`runtime.container_runtime`), for the baseline — without it the baseline is partial and
must be recorded as such.
</integration>

<constraints>
## CONSTRAINTS

1. **`request.md` is verbatim.** Their sentence, their words, their spelling. Add context
   under a separate heading if you must, clearly marked as yours.
2. **Only what decides the next step.** Scope, whether a screen changes, and the parent when
   it is ambiguous. Everything else waits for the stage with the code open.
3. **The title is in their vocabulary**, using the glossary's terms where
   they apply.
4. **The baseline is taken after the branch and before any edit.**
5. **No requirement is written here.** Not one line. That is a separate stage with a
   separate reader.
6. **A recorded non-goal is reported, not routed around.** Quote the non-goal and its
   reason and let the user decide whether to challenge it.
</constraints>

<workflow>
## WORKFLOW

### Phase 1: Capture

- [ ] Take the user's sentence exactly as they wrote it. Keep it for `--request`
- [ ] If they wrote several sentences, keep all of them

### Phase 2: Place it

- [ ] Read the three product documents (Stage 2 above)
- [ ] Is it a recorded **non-goal**? Quote it with its reason and ask whether they want to
      challenge that decision. Do not create a change until they say yes
- [ ] Is it already covered by a specified-but-unbuilt feature in the roadmap? Say so —
      the change may be "build what is already specified", which is a much smaller thing
- [ ] Name it in the glossary's words. `GuestbookEntry` in an identifier, and the same
      concept named the same way in the title

### Phase 2b: Size it — the path (tier)

The pipeline has four paths and the cost difference is an order of magnitude, so
sizing is not optional. Classify from what you already read — **domain facts,
never technology questions** (the user knows their own work, not databases).
First match wins:

- **P0 correction** — no behavior changes at all (copy, a log line, documentation).
- **P3 strategic** — a new business process / bounded context; anything
  changing how money or personal data are handled; a change spanning
  several contexts.
- **P2 standard** — a business rule or calculation changes; a screen or the
  API contract's shape changes; any database migration; blast radius beyond a
  handful of files.
- **P1 minor** — everything else: one behavior, one existing context, no
  migration, no new screen.

Rules of the sizing: this number is **provisional and says so**. `cr-impact`
measures the signals two steps from here, against the actual specification tree,
and `.specconf/process.json` turns them into a path arithmetically — so what you
record is a starting point for a change nobody has read yet, not a verdict.

Recommend the path the request actually implies, and **do not round upwards when
unsure**. That instruction used to be here and it was correct for exactly as long
as lowering a tier was impossible: the safer move was always more process, so every
change drifted up, and a 4-requirement, 143-line change walked the strategic path —
nine stages, 30 dispatches, 24 coherence findings, 40,8 hours. The arithmetic can
now lower a tier on its own when the measured signals agree with it, so a guess that
is one path too small costs a `set-tier` call, while a guess one path too large costs
the whole difference and nobody notices it was wrong.

The recommendation is yours, the confirmation is theirs; never present the tier as
a technical choice — present what it means for THEM. Print the briefing:

```
This looks like a {small} change: {one sentence on what for and why I judge it
so, in the language of the domain}.
Option A — the small path (recommended)
  For: faster and cheaper ({N} stages instead of {M}); the tests and the run from
  nothing stay.
  Against: fewer pairs of eyes over the requirements — should the subject grow,
  the process will propose moving to the full path by itself.
Option B — the standard path
  For: requirements from three independent authors and a full design.
  Against: several times longer; at the scale of this report, usually no gain.

Recommendation: A
Reasoning: {one sentence, about their work}
```

The tier can always be raised later. It is lowered by the measurement — `cr-impact`
records the signals with `sdd-engine change_state set-signals`, and `set-tier` then accepts a
lowering the arithmetic agrees with, without asking anybody. Any OTHER lowering — a
partial measurement, a judgement, a path the arithmetic does not name — still needs
the user and `--allow-lower`. Say this in one sentence when you print the briefing:
the user is confirming a starting point, not signing off a cost.

### Phase 3: Confirm, if you must

Only when the answer changes what happens next. Print the briefing, then ask:

```
Option A — One change
  For: one branch, one set of tests, one deployment.
  Against: there is no way to release half of it earlier.
Option B — Two separate changes
  For: the first can be released and tested straight away.
  Against: twice as much going through the process.

Recommendation: A
Reasoning: {one sentence, about their work}
```

- [ ] Every field through `/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/sdd/hitl_text.py` — a typographic quotation closed
      with a straight `"` terminates the JSON and the question never appears

### Phase 4: Create

```bash
sdd-engine cr new "{title in the user's words}" \
    --request "{verbatim}" --kind {feature|fix|chore} --tier {p0|p1|p2|p3} \
    [--parent CR-YYMM-xxxx] [--touches-ui] [--tracker BI-NNN]
```

- [ ] Read back the `cr_id`, `dir`, `branch` and `input_dir` from its JSON. The scaffold
      has already copied the specification templates into the directory and created the
      `input/` drop-folder
- [ ] For a fix to a merged change: `--parent` names the CR from `spec/changes/INDEX.md`,
      and `cr.py` refuses a parent that does not resolve

### Phase 4b: Tell them what to drop in

Print this, filled in — it mirrors `input/README.md`, which the scaffold wrote:

```
📁 The change has its own directory: spec/changes/{dir}/

Before the specification starts, drop whatever you have into spec/changes/{dir}/input/:
  • requirement notes — in your own words
  • new test data for this case — CSV/XLSX, synthetic data.
    Two kinds, and they are different things: fixtures a test reads, and seed
    data a freshly created environment opens with
  • save a Claude Design mockup as spec/changes/{dir}/design/ui/index.html

The process wants to know at least: what data the change processes (new fields? changes
to existing ones?), the process step by step, a list of test scenarios, the functional
and non-functional requirements and — most important — what this change does NOT do.
The full checklist: spec/changes/{dir}/input/README.md

When you are done, write "go on" or "build the specification". If you drop nothing in,
the process will ask you these questions one by one in conversation.
```

### Phase 5: Baseline

```bash
sdd-engine gate run --profile boundary --json --out .sdd/reports/baseline.json
```

- [ ] **`boundary`, and not `fast`.** `boundary` is the profile that ENDS a stage, so the
      two measure the same keys by construction. `check --fast` reads no suite's junit
      (`reads=()`), so a baseline taken with it records at most `gate:Application check`
      while a boundary observes `<classname>::<case>` — disjoint key spaces, and nothing
      the baseline holds can match anything the boundary sees. That is what made seven
      consecutive closures of `CR-2609-9625` cost a `--accept-red`, five of them over one
      template test that was red before the change existed. It costs the whole of `check`
      here instead of `check --fast`, and that is the price of the baseline being usable
- [ ] `GREEN` → record it as the baseline
- [ ] Not green → record it anyway, with its failures. **This is important:** a red trunk
      is exactly what a baseline is for. Tell the user plainly that something was already
      broken before their change, and that the process will not blame them for it
- [ ] Record it:

```bash
sdd-engine change_state set-baseline --cr {cr_id} --from-file .sdd/reports/baseline.json
```

### Phase 6: Hand over

- [ ] Tell the user: the change exists, which branch it is on, which PATH it
      took and what stages lie ahead (print the progress map:
      `sdd-engine sdd_status`), what to drop into `input/`
      (Phase 4b, if not already printed), and what happens next (someone will look at how
      this works today, then come back with questions)
- [ ] Return the Status Report
</workflow>

<error_handling>
## ERROR HANDLING

| Condition | Action |
|---|---|
| A change already exists on this branch | Not an intake. Hand to the `sdd` orchestrator — the user wants that change continued. |
| The working tree is dirty | STOP. Name the files. A baseline over uncommitted work measures the wrong thing. |
| `cr.py` refuses | Read the message; it is a precondition, not a transient. Do not retry. |
| The request is a recorded non-goal | Report the non-goal and its reason. Create nothing until the user chooses to challenge it. |
| The container daemon is unavailable | Take the baseline at `--profile boundary-no-docker`, record it, and say plainly that it is partial. It reads only the suites this machine can run directly; a boundary that later observes a suite it never measured reports that failure as INCOMPARABLE rather than as this change's. |
| The baseline is red | Record it and say so. That is the baseline doing its job. |
| The user describes a production defect on the trunk | Hand to `sdd-hotfix-scope`. |
</error_handling>

<quality_gate>
## QUALITY GATE


Verification before every declaration of completion: [`/Users/jaroslawwasowski/.claude/plugins/cache/scalo/forge/0.1.126/skills/_shared/verification.md`](../_shared/verification.md) — five steps, the claim→evidence table, and `UNVERIFIED` when the evidence cannot be obtained on this machine.

### Stage 1 — Automated checks

    sdd-skill cr-request preflight

It prints text to read, not JSON to parse. The branch line must say `ok`, the change line
must name the change you just opened, and no `STOP` line may remain.

### Stage 2 — Review before handing over

1. **`request.md` is their words.** STOP if: you can find a sentence in it you wrote and
   did not mark as yours.
2. **The baseline exists and is recorded.** STOP if: `baseline_captured` is false — every
   later verdict compares against nothing.
3. **No requirement was written.** STOP if: `requirements.md` has been filled in — that is,
   if its `TEMPLATE` marker is gone. The scaffold copies the form here at `cr new` (§ Files
   written, above), and a form is not a document: the engine's own readers count a
   marker-bearing file as absent, and so does this gate. What must not have happened is the
   requirements stage, which has not run and has not read the code.
4. **A non-goal was surfaced, if there was one.** STOP if: you created a change for
   something `spec/invariants.md` deliberately excludes without telling the user.
5. **Nothing was asked that does not decide the next step.** STOP if: you interviewed them.
   The requirements stage does that, with the code in front of it. The number itself is the
   engine's — `ask-question` refuses what exceeds the stage's budget.
6. **The user knows what happens next.** STOP if: your last message was about
   branches and records rather than about their change.
</quality_gate>

<bottom_line>
## BOTTOM LINE

**Write down what they said, exactly, in their words. Check it against what the product
deliberately does not do, because a recorded non-goal deserves a conversation rather than a
branch. Ask only what decides the next step — is this one change, and does a screen change — and ask
them as closed questions with a recommendation. Then cut the branch, take the verification
baseline before a single edit, and record it even when it is red, because a red baseline is
precisely what stops this change being blamed for what was already broken. Decide nothing
about scope: that belongs to the stage that will have read the code.**
</bottom_line>

guestbook.md

# Invariants

Things that must always be true. An invariant has no date and no rejected alternative — if it
had one it would be a decision and would belong in [`ADR/`](ADR/).

**These identifiers are load-bearing.** An identifier from here is never renamed or reused; a
superseded invariant keeps its heading and gains a "Superseded by" line. A hole in the
numbering is information, not mess.

**But a hole is information only when what was in it can still be read, and one of them fails
that.** Gate `G9` is cited in this repository solely as a precedent for withdrawal — in
[`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § Scripts, in `stages.py` and in its test —
and **what it held is stated by no document, no comment and no commit**. What is left is the
information "something was here" without the information "what", which is exactly as much as
no entry at all carries. Hence the rule for the next withdrawal: **a withdrawal is recorded
together with one sentence about what the gate held.** `G13` has one (the decision about
POSIX scripts: the `.sh` and `.ps1` twins must change in one diff) and that is the pattern;
`G9` does not, and can no longer be reconstructed.

### The rule, amended for gate names

**An identifier whose subject is fixed by a document is never renamed. A gate name is renamed
only together with a mapping table that keeps every archived citation readable.** The two are
not the same kind of identifier, and treating them as one is what this amendment corrects: an
invariant's number is a handle on a *decision*, while a gate's identifier is a handle on a
*check that still runs* and is read every time it goes red. A handle nobody can decode is a
cost paid on every reading.

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-06, `cr: historical` — the gates were renamed from `G1` to `G20`
into descriptive names, which is the one thing the rule above forbids, so the rule is amended
here rather than quietly broken; framework changes are made on the trunk and carry no
`delta.md` in which to declare the edit):

- **Rename without amending this rule.** The rename would then stand as a violation of a
  document saying it cannot happen — which teaches that the rules here are advisory, and that
  is more expensive than any gate name.
- **Rename and drop the old codes from history.** The audits under `spec/rationale/` and the
  notes under `retro/` record what was true on a date. Rewriting their nouns makes them agree
  with today at the cost of no longer being records.
- **Extend "never renamed" to cover gates explicitly, and keep the numbers.** Consistent, and
  it settles the cost in exactly the wrong direction: the identifiers a person reads most
  often would be the ones guaranteed to stay unreadable.

Consequences: gate names are the single renameable identifier space in this repository, and the
price of that is the mapping table in
[the process's `spec_gates.py`](https://github.com/Scalo-Sales-Engineering-Consulting/claude-marketplace/blob/main/plugins/forge/skills/_shared/sdd/spec_gates.py), where every gate declares the code it
carried, held to the register by `test_sdd_spec_lint.py`. `D-*`, `R-*`, `CR-*` and the headings in this file are
unchanged: never renamed, never reused.

Rejected (decision of 2026-09-10, `cr: historical` — the forge plugin deleted its `docs/` tree
on 2026-09-10 and kept only what the process runs on, so `sdd-reference.md` and its table of
old numeric codes exist nowhere; the mapping from a retired code to a gate's name lives in the
gate register itself, `spec_gates.py`, where every gate declares the code it carried, and the
links here name that. Framework changes are made on the trunk and carry no `delta.md`): leaving
links that return 404, or copying the mapping into this document — the second home this section
argues against.

**What this file holds today.** Deliberate non-goals and the rule about the rules themselves —
the things that have no version. The data invariants `D-01`…`D-03` moved out to
[`contracts/invariants/guestbook.md`](../contracts/invariants/guestbook.md); the section below
says why.

---

## Data invariants

**Moved to [`contracts/invariants/guestbook.md`](../contracts/invariants/guestbook.md),
2026-09-02.** The identifiers `D-01`…`D-03` were not renamed or reused and will not be — after
this change the `D-*` space has a single owner.

What they held, one sentence each, so the hole can be read without opening the other file —
the rule at the top of this document demands exactly that:

- **`D-01`** — a domain entity has one row from creation to end, not a copy in an "archive
  sheet", where history is destroyed by separation rather than by deletion.
- **`D-02`** — a fact belonging to another entity is pointed at, not transcribed; the
  exception is a deliberate historical snapshot, which has to be named as one.
- **`D-03`** — every primary key is a UUID generated on the application side, never a number
  from a sequence ([`design/data-model.md`](design/data-model.md) § Identifiers).

**Why they left.** A data invariant is a statement about a system boundary — about what may be
relied on without looking inside — and a boundary is a versioned contract (constitution,
article VI). This file stayed with what has no version: the rule about the rules themselves,
and the deliberate non-goals.

**The move closed, in passing, a gap this section used to admit outright.** The previous
wording said that `D-01`…`D-03` were held by the data model and by the decision about UUIDs,
"rather than by a test that names them". The new home does not accept an invariant without a
`**Witness:**` and a `**Kind of evidence:**` line, and the witnesses exist: sweepers over
`Base.metadata` in `tests/fitness/test_data_invariants.py` and a property with a generator in
`tests/unit/test_data_invariant_properties.py`.

**The editing route has not changed, and does not change for either half.** The rule from
§ Deliberate non-goals — "every edit to this file within a change cycle belongs to the
convergence round" — is inherited by the new home: the write set of `review-converge` covers
`contracts/` for the same reason it covers `spec/`.

---

## Deliberate non-goals

Standing product decisions, not oversights: they bind every change exactly as an invariant
does, and that is why they live here. Adding any one of them is a change with its own
requirements, not a gap somebody spotted.

**Lifting a non-goal has one route, and that route is written here, because its absence cost
four authors of one stage.** A non-goal is lifted by **a human decision recorded in a change
record** (question and answer in `requirements.md`), and an ADR names it only when it is
cross-cutting ([`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § When a decision is an ADR).
The striking-out is done by the **stage's convergence round**, in this file and in the same PR
as the code, because the author of a design document does not have this path in their write
set — and does not have it deliberately: a document standing above `spec/design/**` cannot be
changed by what stands below it. A lifted item **stays** with its heading and gains a "lifted
by `<CR>`" line together with its former wording; it is never renamed or deleted.

**This route applies to the whole file, not only to the striking-out.** **Every edit to
`spec/invariants.md` within a change cycle** belongs to the convergence round — lifting a
non-goal, adding an invariant, fixing a broken cross-reference. No fan-out author gets this
path in their write set; an author who sees a divergence here **reports it as a finding and
does not try to fix it**. The rule is in this wording because the previous one — written from

# Changes

One row per change. A change is one directory here, one branch and one `change.json` —
the authority on that change's state.

This table is for people. The machine's answer to the same question is
[`status.json`](status.json), generated from the same records in the same run and read
by scripts through `registry.py` rather than by opening the file.

`status` is `draft` until a change is ready to merge, then `ready`, then `merged`. A
merged change **stays where it is**: the directory is its permanent address, and a later
hotfix finds the requirements and design it needs by looking up the parent in this table.

A change abandoned or superseded *before* merging also stays in place, with
`status: abandoned` — the registry filters it out of the open set, and the directory
keeps its reasoning, because a dead end is expensive knowledge.

# Glossary

Domain words used across the repository, with the source form that is the identifier in the
code. A term that means something **only inside one context** lives in that context's
document, not here — today there is one context, so the split is an exercise for the future,
but the rule holds from the first day.

The language rule behind this: the whole repository is written in English, and a **domain term
keeps its source form inside an identifier** — so that a field can be grepped from a sentence
in the specification to a column in the database (`spec/design/conventions.md` § Language).

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Guestbook** | The only bounded context of this system. The set of entries left by guests. |
| **Entry** | One utterance by a guest: a signature, a message, the moment it was written and the moment it was last amended. The smallest thing this system stores. Table `guestbook_entries`. |
| **Author** | What the guest signed with. **It is not an identity** — the system authenticates nobody, so a signature is a claim rather than a statement of fact. Column `author`. |
| **Message** | What the guest wrote. Column `message`. |
| **Edited** | An entry whose moment of last amendment differs from its moment of writing. A fact **derived** by comparing `created_at` and `updated_at`, never stored (`BR-02`). |

## Process words, not domain words

They live here because they come up in every conversation about this repository and get
confused with domain words.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Bounded context** | A slice of the domain with its own vocabulary and its own document under `spec/contexts/`. The same word is allowed to mean different things in two contexts; that is the entire reason the boundary exists. |
| **Strategic classification** | What a context is worth: **core** is what the product competes on, **supporting** is specific to this business but not a differentiator, **generic** is what you would buy if somebody sold it. Declared as `classification` in a context document's front matter, and it decides how much modelling a context deserves. |
| **Integration pattern** | What one context does about another's model at the seam — an anti-corruption layer translates it, a conformist adopts it whole, an open host service publishes one. Declared per neighbour as `<context>:<role>:<pattern>`; the legal pairings and the reason they are the legal ones are in [`../.specconf/templates/system/context.md`](../.specconf/templates/system/context.md) § Neighbours. A boundary recorded only as a direction says who calls whom and not what breaks when they change. |
| **Golden set** | `golden-set/` — the only home of committed data this project ships, cut in two by what the data is for: **fixtures** and **seed data** (both below). One locator, `tests/_golden_set.py`, decides where either half lies. |
| **Fixtures (the fixture half)** | `golden-set/fixtures/` — what the suites read instead of inventing, and assert about: ordinary, boundary and refused entries. Wiped before every scenario. |
| **Seed data (the seed half)** | `golden-set/seed/` — what a freshly created environment opens with, so a preview or a fresh clone shows a screen somebody can judge. Posted through the application's own API by `scripts/seed.sh`; asserted about by nothing, which `tests/fitness/test_golden_set.py` enforces. |
| **Escape hatch** | Historical: SQLite as the database for a machine without Docker. Removed 2026-08-31 ([`design/architecture.md`](design/architecture.md) § One engine) — today such a machine points at its own Postgres through `APP_TEST_DATABASE_URL`. The term stays, because archived change records still read it. |
| **Fitness function** | A test that reads **this repository's source as text**, to hold a structural rule no compiler enforces. `tests/fitness/`. |
| **sdd107** | An external text on ownership-first architecture the author drew on when cutting the tree by bounded context; cited in `design/conventions.md` § Backend, `design/architecture.md` and `.github/CODEOWNERS`. **It is not in this repository and cannot be checked from it** (found by the 2026-09-08 audit): the reasoning written beside each citation is this repository's own and is meant to stand without it, so the name is an attribution, not an authority. |
| **Session** | In this repository **always** a SQLAlchemy unit of work (`SessionLocal`). There is no user session, because there is no authentication — and when the product adds one, this is exactly the trap to name: two different concepts, one word. |

## Identifiers and their spaces

Every space has exactly one home in which a citation resolves. The `frozen-ids` gate holds this for
the first five spaces below — an identifier named in prose and defined nowhere goes red. A change
id and a requirement id are held by the change record and `traceability` instead.

| Space | Means | Home |
|---|---|---|
| `P-xx` | a flow within a context | `spec/contexts/<context>.md` |
| `BR-xx` | a business rule | `spec/contexts/<context>.md` |
| `S-xx` | a screen | front matter of `spec/design/ui/<screen>.md` |
| `D-xx` | a data invariant | `contracts/invariants/<domain>.md` |
| `ADR-xxxx` | a dated decision from a change record | `spec/ADR/` (empty today — [`design/conventions.md`](design/conventions.md) § When a decision is an ADR) |
| `CR-YYMM-xxxx` | a change | `spec/changes/` |
| `CR-YYMM-xxxx/R-n` | a requirement of a change | that change's `requirements.md` |

Utworzyłem zmianę dla listy zadań. Zanim przejdę dalej, musisz zatwierdzić zapis prośby.

**Co jest gotowe**
- Zmiana: **CR-2609-823a** („Todo list – add tasks and mark them done”) na gałęzi `sdd/CR-2609-823a-todo-list-add-tasks-and-mark-them-done`.
- Twoja prośba jest zapisana słowo w słowo w `spec/changes/CR-2609-823a-todo-list-add-tasks-and-mark-them-done/request.md`.
- Ścieżka: pełna (P3), bo to nowy obszar systemu obok księgi gości. Etapy: przyjęcie → wymagania → projekt → plan pracy → implementacja → uruchomienie od zera → uzgodnienie specyfikacji → dostarczenie.
- Twoja prośba nie łamie żadnej zapisanej decyzji produktowej. Brak logowania pasuje do założenia, że każdy może dodawać, odhaczać, edytować i usuwać zadania.

**Stan testów przed zmianą nie był zielony.** Zapisałem go jako punkt odniesienia, więc te błędy nie będą przypisane tej zmianie:
- Testy backendu (748), frontendu (213) i testy struktury (339) przechodzą.
- Pełny `check.sh` nie przeszedł, a testy e2e nie zebrały ani jednego przypadku. Wygląda na problem ze środowiskiem Dockera, ale jeszcze tego nie sprawdzałem.
- Nie przeszły dwie bramki specyfikacji. „One change at a time”: w rejestrze wciąż jest otwarta zmiana **CR-2609-8ef9** (chore, `draft`), a teraz doszła nowa. „Generated indexes”: indeks zmian nie zawiera jeszcze nowej zmiany. Pierwsza z nich może później blokować zamknięcie etapów, więc warto zdecydować, co zrobić z CR-2609-8ef9.

**Możesz coś dorzucić (nieobowiązkowe)** do `spec/changes/CR-2609-823a-todo-list-add-tasks-and-mark-them-done/input/`:
- notatki o wymaganiach, np. maksymalna długość zadania, kolejność listy, czy zadania zrobione mają się chować;
- przykładowe dane testowe (tylko syntetyczne);
